title: Alekhine's Defense
description: A wild approach to White's most popular move, 1.e4. This opening will surprise your opponent and provoke them into a massive battle. A bit tricky to handle for beginners due to the nature of the positions, but great beyond that.

lessons.title: White Plays e5, d4, and c4

r1bq1rk1/ppp1bppp/1nnp4/8/2PP4/2NB4/PP2N.text:
White castles their king.

We have to get developed somehow, and ...Bg4 is the most logical here, even if f3 comes.

r2q1rk1/ppp1bpp1/1nnp2p1/8/2PP4/1PN1BP2/.text: The c4-pawn was under attack, so White supports it with the b-pawn.

r2q1rk1/ppp1bppp/1nnp2B1/8/2PP4/2N1BP2/P.text:
White trades the bishops.

We'll recapture towards the center.

r2q1rk1/ppp1bppp/1nnp4/7b/2PP4/2NBBP2/PP.text:
White develops their final minor piece and adds support to d4.

Let's go for the trade now.

r2q1rk1/ppp1bppp/1nnp4/7b/2PP4/3BBN1P/PP.text:
White develops their knight to d2, supporting c4 and the f3-knight.

The d4-pawn is a target, and we hit it with Bf6!

r2q1rk1/ppp1bppp/1nnp4/8/2PP2b1/2NB1N1P/.text:
White can also delay Be3 and throw in h3, attacking our bishop.

We should yet again maintain the pin.

r2q1rk1/ppp1bppp/1nnp4/8/2PP2b1/2NB1P2/P.text:
White goes f3, breaking the pin.

The g6-square will serve nicely for our bishop — trading off White's active d3-bishop.

r2q1rk1/ppp1bppp/1nnp4/8/2PP2b1/2NBBN2/P.text:
Most natural is Be3, developing a minor piece and defending d4.

We'll add another attacker to the d4-pawn.

r2q1rk1/ppp1bppp/1nnp4/8/2PP4/2NQ1N1P/PP.text:
White moves their king to safety.

We'll improve the bishop and pressure the d4-pawn.

r2q1rk1/ppp2pp1/1nnp1bp1/8/2PP4/1PN1BP2/.text:
And we simply improve our bishop.

The plan here is to bring the rook to the open file and advance ...d5.

r2q1rk1/ppp2pp1/1nnp1bp1/8/2PP4/4BN1P/PP.text:
And we recapture with the h-pawn.

We'll proceed with ...Re8 and ...d5.

r2q1rk1/ppp2ppp/1n1p1b2/3P4/2n3b1/2N1BN2.text:
And now we take the c4-pawn.

Many of your games will go like this. We're simply up a pawn and have a comfortable advantage.

r2q1rk1/ppp2ppp/1n1p1b2/3Pn3/2P3b1/2N1BN.text:
White has to go for damage control with Be2, supporting the f3-knight.

The c4-pawn is now completely free.

r2q1rk1/ppp2ppp/1nnp1b2/3P4/2P3b1/2NBBN2.text:
Most often, White deals with the threat by advancing their d-pawn.

Although White saves the d4-pawn by pushing it, this move is also a concession, as it leaves the e5-square open for our knight.

r2q1rk1/ppp2ppp/1nnp1b2/7b/2PP4/2NBBN1P/.text:
And we go ...Bf6, putting some more pressure on the d4-pawn.

White is fine according to the engine, but we've got great pressure and holding everything together isn't trivial for White.

r2q1rk1/ppp2ppp/1nnp1b2/7b/2PP4/3BBN1P/P.text:
White goes Qc2, unpinning the f3-knight and attacking the h7-pawn.

The bishop on h5 isn't useful anymore, so we can retreat and block the attack on h7.

r2q1rk1/ppp2ppp/1nnp1b2/8/2PP4/2NQBN1P/P.text: White develops their bishop and adds some extra support to d4.

r2qr1k1/ppp2ppp/1nnp1b2/8/2PP4/2NQBN1P/P.text:
We bring our rook to the open file.

This is the position that you can expect to get if White prevents ...Bg4 and trades the bishops. 

...d5 is what we want to be going for in these positions. The inclusion of ...Nb4 is also often quite useful.

rn1q1rk1/ppp1b1pp/1n1p2p1/8/2PP2P1/2N2N1.text:
And we recapture with the f-pawn!

We are doing quite well here. The c4-pawn is hanging, and we've got the semi-open f-file to work with.

rn1q1rk1/ppp1bppp/1n1p4/5b2/2PP4/2N2N1P/.text:
White's other option is Be2.

The light-squared bishops do stay on the board this way, but that doesn't alter our plan all that much.

We'll bring our rook to the open e-file.

rn1q1rk1/ppp1bppp/1n1p4/5b2/2PP4/2NB1N1P.text:
More often, White goes Bd3, offering a trade of bishops.

We'll accept.

rn1q1rk1/ppp1bppp/1n1p4/7b/2PP2P1/2NB1N1.text:
White can also lash out with g4, looking to neutralize the pin.

The bishop drops back.

rn1q1rk1/ppp1bppp/1n1p4/7b/2PP4/3BBN1P/P.text:
White develops their dark-squared bishop and adds support to d4.

We now add some pressure to the d4-pawn.

rn1q1rk1/ppp1bppp/1n1p4/8/2PP2b1/2NB1N1P.text:
Instead of simply castling, White can go h3, attacking our bishop.

We'll go for the usual ...Bh5 to g6 maneuver.

rn1q1rk1/ppp1bppp/1n1p4/8/2PP2b1/2NB1N2/.text:
White castles their king.

The d4-pawn is essentially unprotected, so it's time to attack it.

rn1q1rk1/ppp1bppp/1n1p4/8/2PP4/2NQ1N1P/P.text:
White recaptures.

Let's continue developing the queenside.

rn1qk2r/ppp1bppp/1n1p4/7b/2PP4/3B1N1P/PP.text:
White castles their king.

Let's get our king into safety as well.

rn1qk2r/ppp1bppp/1n1p4/8/2PP2b1/3B1N1P/P.text:
White challenges our bishop.

We should maintain the pin.

rn1qr1k1/ppp1bppp/1n1p4/5b2/2PP4/2N2N1P/.text: White moves their king to safety.

rnbq1rk1/ppp1bppp/1n1p4/8/2PP4/2N2N1P/PP.text:
White can also prevent ...Bg4.

This isn't very common, but it's important for us to analyze since we do have to alter our game-plan.

We'll bring the bishop to f5 instead.

rnbq1rk1/ppp1bppp/1n1p4/8/2PP4/2NB1N2/PP.text:
White develops their light-squared bishop to d3, preparing castling.

Now it's important to pin the knight on f3, which is the main defender of White's center.

rnbq1rk1/ppp1bppp/1n1p4/8/2PP4/2NB4/PP2N.text:
White develops their knight.

We'll also develop.

rnbqk2r/ppp1bppp/1n1p4/8/2PP4/2N2N2/PP3P.text:
White develops their other knight.

Let's get our king into safety.

rnbqk2r/ppp1bppp/1n1p4/8/2PP4/2NB4/PP3PP.text:
Instead of Nf3, White can also go for the setup with Bd3 and Nge2.

The simple idea behind Nge2 is to be able to meet ...Bg4 with f3.

We'll castle.

rnbqk2r/ppp1bppp/1n1p4/8/2PP4/3B1N2/PP3P.text:
White develops their light-squared bishop to d3, preparing castling.

The bishop has developed, so it's time to pin the knight now.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/1n1P4/8/2PP4/8/PP3PPP/.text:
White releases the tension.

This is played almost half the time.

We'll capture with the e-pawn.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/3p4/3nP3/2PP4/8/PP3PPP.text:
White plays c4, taking even more space and attacking our knight.

Our knight will retreat and later help in undermining the center.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/1n1p4/8/2PP4/2N5/PP3PPP.text:
White's first option is to develop their queenside knight to c3.
This is played 43% of the time.

We continue with natural development and aim to castle kingside.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/1n1p4/8/2PP4/5N2/PP3PPP.text:
White's other option is 6. Nf3.

The only notable and unique thing about this move order is that White can go for Nbd2 instead of Nc3.

Our developmental plan against this setup is more or less the same.

First of all, we'll get our bishops out.

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/5n2/4P3/8/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
White pushes e5 and attacks our knight, which is the most principled continuation.

Our idea in the Alekhine is to give White a big center in order to attack and undermine it later on.

We play our knight into the center of the board.

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/8/3nP3/3P4/8/PPP2PPP/R.text:
White advances d4, taking more space and supporting the e-pawn.

Let's start undermining the center.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
Welcome to the first chapter of this course about Alekhine's Defense!

Let's check out White's setup of three pawns — e5, d4 and c4.

White starts with the King's pawn. 

We'll reply with 1...Nf6 — the Alekhine.

lessons.title: White Plays e5, d4, c4, f4

1r2kb1r/p1p2ppp/1n2p3/4P3/2PnB3/8/PP4PP/.text:
White retreats to e4 to stop our knight hopping into c2.

The c4-pawn simply falls.

1r2kb1r/p1p2ppp/4p3/4P3/2nnB3/1P6/P5PP/R.text: And after a move like b3...

1r2kb1r/p1p2ppp/4p3/4n3/3nB3/1P6/P5PP/RN.text:
The e5-pawn falls as well.

We are up two pawns and completely winning.

2kr1b1r/ppp1pQpp/1n6/4q3/2P5/2N5/PP2B1PP.text:
White wants to recover some material.

It makes sense for us to play ...e6 and open up the bishop on f8.

2kr1b1r/ppp2Qpp/1n2p3/4q3/2P5/2N5/PP2B1P.text:
White castles.

We'll develop with check!

2kr1r2/ppp2Qpp/1n2p3/2b1q3/2P5/2N5/PP2B1.text:
White has to retreat their queen to h5.

We can trade the queens and go for the endgame with up a pawn!

2kr3r/ppp2Qpp/1n2p3/2b1q3/2P5/2N5/PP2B1P.text: The king moves out of check.

3r1rk1/ppp1q1pp/1nn1pb2/5b2/2PP4/2N1BN2/.text:
And we improve the rook to d8.

Our plans include preparing to push ...e5 and also ...Nb4-c2 and going for ...c5 break.

Before pushing for ...e5, we can first play ...h6 and retreat the bishop to h7, so that after ...e5 it isn't undefended.

3rkb1r/p1p1pppp/1nQ5/4P3/2Pq4/8/PP4PP/RN.text:
White gives a check.

We block with the rook.

4k2r/p1pr1ppp/1nQ1p3/2b1P3/2Pq4/2N5/PP2B.text:
And we threaten a checkmate on f2! 

White's dark-squares are critically weak, and the c4-pawn is a target.

4kb1r/p1prpppp/1nQ5/4P3/2Pq4/8/PP2B1PP/R.text:
White covers their king with the bishop.

We'll play e6 and prepare to bring our bishop into the attack.

r1bqkb1r/ppp1pppp/1nn5/4P3/2PP4/4B3/PP4P.text:
This is the strongest move, but played only 30% of the time.

Our bishop will find a nice square on f5.

r1bqkb1r/ppp1pppp/1nn5/4P3/2PP4/5N2/PP4P.text:
White develops seemingly naturally in about 60% of the games, but this move isn't very good.

It allows us to create an annoying pin, which yet again undermines White's center.

r2q1rk1/ppp1b1pp/1nn1pP2/5b2/2PP4/2N1BN2.text:
White trades - otherwise they would be left with a weak pawn on e5.

We'll grab with the bishop.

r2q1rk1/ppp1bppp/1nn1p3/4Pb2/2PP4/2N1BN2.text:
White castles as well.

Now it's time to undermine White's pawn structure.

r2q1rk1/ppp3pp/1nn1pb2/5b2/2PP4/2N1BN2/P.text:
White connects the rooks.

With ...Qe7 we can connect ours as well.

r2qk2r/ppp1bppp/1nn1p3/4P3/2PP4/2N1BP2/P.text: White would like to castle queenside.

r2qk2r/ppp1bppp/1nn1p3/4Pb2/2PP4/2N1BN2/.text:
White prepares to castle.

Let's get the king into safety.

r2qk2r/ppp2ppp/1nn1p3/4P3/2PP3b/2N1BP2/P.text:
But now we give a check! 

White has to move the king and lose their castling rights, as Bf2 would drop the important d4-pawn.

Both ...O-O followed by ...f6 or, alternatively, ...Qd7/...Qe7 followed by ...O-O-O are very good in this positions.

r2qkb1r/pQp1pppp/1n6/4P3/2P5/4B3/PPn2KPP.text:
The king moves.

Now there is no need to capture the rook.

We grab the bishop and lure out White's king even further!

r2qkb1r/pQp1pppp/1n6/4P3/2Pn4/4B3/PP4PP/.text:
You might also occasionally encounter Qxb7 here.

We'll give a check on c2.

r2qkb1r/pQp2ppp/1n2p3/4P3/2P5/4K3/PP4PP/.text:
White's king is very exposed and Black is doing great here with ...Bc5 coming.

Even if Qc6+ comes, we can go for a queen trade and enjoy a position with the better development.

r2qkb1r/ppp1pppp/1n6/4P3/2PB4/5Q2/PP4PP/.text:
White trades off the strong knight.

We recapture.

r2qkb1r/ppp1pppp/1nn5/4P3/2PP2b1/4BN2/PP.text:
White supports d4.

Usually, Black gets rid of the knight that defends the center.

r2qkb1r/ppp1pppp/1nn5/4P3/2PP2b1/5N2/PP2.text:
White can block the pin with the bishop, but they have to be careful.

Now we develop and cover the d5-square by playing ...e6.

r2qkb1r/ppp1pppp/1nn5/4P3/2PP4/4BP2/PP5P.text:
White recaptures with the g-pawn, planning to strengthen the structure with a later f4.

Our dark-squared bishop could use some air. Let's play e6.

r2qkb1r/ppp1pppp/1nn5/4P3/2PP4/4BQ2/PP4P.text:
White captures on f3 with the queen, occurring in 25% of the games.

We can grab a pawn on d4 now!

r2qkb1r/ppp1pppp/1nn5/4Pb2/2PP4/2N1B3/PP.text:
White develops the queenside knight.

Let's stabilize the central squares.

r2qkb1r/ppp2ppp/1nn1p3/4P3/2PP2b1/5N2/PP.text:
For example, castling here ultimately loses the game.

The d4-pawn is weak. Capturing on f3 weakens it further.

r2qkb1r/ppp2ppp/1nn1p3/4P3/2PP4/2N1BP2/P.text:
White develops the knight.

Their king is a bit open, so let's start eyeing it.

r2qkb1r/ppp2ppp/1nn1p3/4P3/2PP4/5B2/PP4P.text:
White recaptures.

The d4-pawn is now free to grab with a check!

r2qkb1r/ppp2ppp/1nn1p3/4Pb2/2PP4/2N1BN2/.text:
White develops the second knight.

We'll answer by preparing to castle.

r3kb1r/pBp2ppp/1n2p3/4P3/2Pn4/8/PP4PP/RN.text:
Sure, White can get back one pawn.

But with d4 falling, the whole structure in the center is loose.

We'll hit the bishop with our rook, gaining time.

r3kb1r/pQp1pppp/1n6/4P3/2Pq4/8/PP4PP/RN2.text:
White goes for the b7-pawn.

But with ...Rd8 we create a strong battery on the d-file.

r3kb1r/ppp1pppp/1n6/4P3/2Pq4/2N2Q2/PP4PP.text:
White doesn't go pawn hunting but develops instead.

We take on e5 with check.

r3kb1r/ppp1pppp/1n6/4q3/2P5/2N2Q2/PP2B1P.text:
White wants to keep their castling rights, so they interpose.

We castle queenside.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/1n1p4/4P3/2PP1P2/8/PP4.text:
Close to 30% of games go like this: almost 2 million games in the database! 

White is building up their center, and now is the perfect time to trade on e5 and force White to make a decision.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/1n6/4P3/2PP4/8/PP4PP/R.text:
White doesn't want to go for a queen trade so they recapture with the f-pawn.

Let's start adding pressure to e5 and d4.

Developing the queen's knight to c6 is the perfect way to do this.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/3p4/3nP3/2PP4/8/PP3PPP.text:
White attacks our knight.

We'll retreat.

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/5n2/4P3/8/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
More than half of the time White attacks our knight here.

Let's bring the knight into the center.

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/8/3nP3/3P4/8/PPP2PPP/R.text:
White puts another pawn in the center.

Now we start undermining it.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
Welcome to the second chapter of the Alekhine! 

In this line, White opts for a seemingly dangerous four pawns attack with d4, c4 and f4. 

Let's take a look at how to undermine White's central expansion!

White starts with the King's Pawn opening.

And we reply with Nf6, the Alekhine.

lessons.title: White Plays e5, d4, c4, and Nf3

r1b1kb1r/ppp1p2p/1Pn2pp1/4q3/8/5Q2/PP2BP.text:
We'll develop to c6 with the threat of ...Nd4.

Black is winning.

r1b1kb1r/ppp1p3/1Pn2pp1/4q3/8/5Q2/PP2BPP.text:
And we don't even have to recapture the pawn right away.

Activating the knight to c6 threatens ...Nd4 which would be devastating.

Besides, development comes first and now we've got a much more active position and a huge advantage.

r1bq1rk1/p1p1ppbp/1np3p1/8/2PP4/2N1B3/PP.text:
White will look to do the same.

But the white center is a target in this position.

r1bqk2r/p1p1ppbp/1np3p1/8/2PP4/2N1B3/PP3.text:
White defends by retreating the bishop.

A rather passive move that allows us to get our king into safety.

r1bqk2r/ppp1ppbp/1nN3p1/8/2PP1B2/2N5/PP3.text:
White will probably accept at this point to double our pawns.

However, we will take that to our advantage. The d4-pawn is soft.

r2q1rk1/p1p1ppbp/1n2b1p1/2p5/2PP4/1PN1B3.text:
We can use our doubled c-pawn to attack the center!

White can't capture or push because of the weak knight on c3.

Black is on the verge of being winning here.

r2q1rk1/p1p1ppbp/1np1b1p1/8/2PP4/1PN1B3/.text:
White has basically no choice but to defend with b3.

That obviously weakens the knight on c3 and gives us an idea.

rn1qk2r/pp2ppbp/2p1b1p1/2PNN3/2BP4/5Q2/P.text:
White trades.

We'll recapture with the bishop first.

rn1qk2r/pp2ppbp/2p3p1/2PBN3/3P4/5Q2/PP3P.text:
They can choose to trade all the way.

We have to recapture with the queen now, to cover f7.

rn1qk2r/ppp1ppbp/4b1p1/2PnN3/2BP4/2N2Q2/.text: Now White offers a trade, but we'll keep protecting the knight.

rn2k2r/pp2ppbp/2p3p1/2PQN3/3P4/8/PP3PPP/.text: Even if the queens get traded...

rn2k2r/pp2ppbp/6p1/2PpN3/3P4/8/PP3PPP/R1.text:
We'll recapture and have a lot of potential in the upcoming endgame.

Trading the bishop for the knight and then chipping away at White's split pawns is actually a great plan.

We don't want them to have healthy central control.

In this version with the White pawn on c5, Black is better.

rnb1kb1r/ppp1p2p/1P3pp1/4N3/3q4/5Q2/PP3P.text: If White captures the knight, we'll grab on e5 with a check.

rnb1kb1r/ppp1p2p/1P3pp1/4q3/8/5Q2/PP2BPP.text: The bishop blocks, and we've got a motif we also see in the 9.Nxg6 line.

rnb1kb1r/ppp1p2p/1n3pN1/2P5/3q4/5Q2/PP3P.text:
White's got an intermezzo here, but it doesn't do much.

We just take.

rnb1kb1r/ppp1p3/1P3pp1/8/3q4/5Q2/PP3PPP/.text:
White regains the piece.

We can now get our queen into a better position.

rnbqk2r/ppp1ppbp/1n4p1/4N3/2PP1B2/2N5/PP.text:
White protects the knight.

Let's offer a trade.

rnbqk2r/ppp1ppbp/6p1/2PnN3/2BP4/5Q2/PP3P.text:
White now attacks both the f7-pawn and the knight on f5. 

We've got a move that stops both threats.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1p2p/1n3pp1/2P1N3/3P4/5Q2/PP.text: If White counterattacks the knight, we can leave the tension as it is and capture in the center.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pp1p/1n4p1/2P1N3/3P4/8/PP3P.text:
One of the possible moves is c5, although I doubt you will encounter it very often.

White attacks the knight again but over-extends a bit and allows our knight to jump back to d5.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pp1p/1n4p1/4N3/2PP4/2N5/PP3.text:
Another move they can choose to play is Nc3, simply continuing development without any attack on the f7-pawn.

We'll simply continue with our fianchetto plan.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pp1p/1n4p1/4N3/2PP4/5Q2/PP3.text:
One way to do that is to create a checkmate threat on the f7-square.

It might seem uncomfortable defending this, but don't be afraid of playing ...f6.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pp1p/6p1/2PnN3/2BP4/8/PP3PP.text:
However, this was White's point behind c4 — to eyeball the f7-pawn with the bishop.

So let's keep the knight on d5 and get developed.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/1n1p4/4P3/2PP4/5N2/PP3.text:
And now White chooses to activate the knight.

There could be a lot of transpositions here, but the main point is that we can now capture on e5.

This move is played 14% of the time, equal to almost 850,000 games.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/1n6/4N3/2PP4/8/PP3PPP/.text:
White takes with the knight to keep the center together, which is one of the reasons they developed it on move 5.

I recommend ...g6 with a fianchetto to start developing our pieces.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/3p4/3nP3/2PP4/8/PP3PPP.text:
White goes after our knight again.

b6 is a safe square for it.

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/5n2/4P3/8/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
The most common move, attacking our knight.

Let's get the knight into the center.

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/8/3nP3/3P4/8/PPP2PPP/R.text:
White supports the e5-pawn and prepares c4.

Now Black tries to chip away at the e5-pawn.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
In this chapter, we'll focus on a specific but rare set of moves by White.

That is the d4, c4 and Nf3 setup.

With this approach, White is still aggressive towards our knight in the opening but opts to develop and let us capture on e5 if we want to.

White opens with 1.e4, and we'll reply with the Alekhine's, 1...Nf6.

lessons.title: Lines with d4 and not c4

r2q1rk1/pp1nppbp/2p1b1p1/3nN3/2BP4/2P2N2.text:
What White can do instead is support the knight with the other one.

That's why they played Nd2 in the first place.

However, try to spot a future tactic here.

If the white knights got exchanged off, we could capture on c3 with tempo, and the bishop on c4 would be undefended.

r2q1rk1/pp2pp1p/2p1b1p1/3nR3/2BP4/2P5/PP.text: The rook recaptures, and we unleash our tactic.

r2q1rk1/pp2pp1p/2p1b1p1/4R3/2BP4/2P5/P4P.text:
White's queen was attacked, so they had to capture the knight.

Now we regain the piece by grabbing on c4.

r2q1rk1/pp2pp1p/2p3p1/4R3/2bP4/B1P5/P4PP.text:
An active move you have to be careful for is Ba3 here.

White attacks our weak spot on e7.

r2q1rk1/pp2ppbp/2p1b1p1/3nN3/2BP4/2P5/PP.text:
Logical for White to recapture with the knight.

They hadn't accounted for our tactic, though. First, we trade on e5.

r2qkb1r/pp1Npppp/2p5/5b2/1nPP4/N3B3/PP3P.text:
Trading keeps the position in the balance.

We'll recapture with the queen, and normal development will follow.

r2qkb1r/pp1n1ppp/2p5/4Nb2/1nPP4/N3B3/PP3.text:
White captures with the knight now.

We recapture, but It seems like we've given up the pawn on e5.

r2qkb1r/pp1npppp/2p5/5b2/1nPP4/N2NB3/PP3.text:
Retreating to d3 and trying to trade for our active knight loses the game.

This is a move you have to remember.

We strike in the center with ...e5!

Now the center is under attack, the knight is protected and White's options are limited.

r2qkb1r/pp3ppp/2p5/4Pb2/1nP5/N3B3/PP3PPP.text:
But once White captures, here's our trick.

The move ...Qa5 is actually crushing.

The queen targets the e5-pawn and sets up a discovered check on the king at the same time.

This move would have worked if White had captured with the pawn on move 10 as well.

r2qr1k1/pp2pp1p/2p3p1/4R3/2bP4/B1P5/P4PP.text:
Luckily, the simple ...Re8 defends it.

In the end, Black is slightly better being up a pawn.

However, the bishops are of different colors and White has maintained some activity.

White definitely has drawing chances.

r3k2r/pp1q1ppp/2pbp3/5b2/1nPP4/N3B3/PP2B.text: And we'll develop our bishop to its most active square, with the intention of castling.

r3kb1r/pp1qpppp/2p5/5b2/1nPP4/N3B3/PP2BP.text:
The bishop comes out to e2 and White is ready to castle.

We'll open up the dark-squared bishop, with similar ideas.

r3kb1r/pp3ppp/2p5/4qb2/1nP5/N7/PP1BQPPP/.text:
Once the queen blocks...

We've got a check on d3, which is key.

The pawns on b2 and f2 are also under fire.

r3kb1r/pp3ppp/2p5/4qb2/2P5/N2n4/P2BQPPP/.text:
Now the king moves back to d1.

We could simply take on a3 and be a piece up, but there is even better!

r3kb1r/pp3ppp/2p5/4qb2/2P5/N2n4/PP1BQPPP.text:
The king slides to d1.

We can take on b2 with check.

r3kb1r/pp3ppp/2p5/4qb2/2P5/N7/P2BQnPP/R3.text:
Instead, White slides to e1.

Black is winning in multiple different ways here.

You can trade queens and capture the rook on h1 or simply play ...Ne4 back.

The game should soon be over.

r3kb1r/pp3ppp/2p5/4qb2/2P5/N7/Pn1BQPPP/R.text:
Whichever move the king makes, it doesn't help White's case at all.

We'll simply jump back to d3.

r3kb1r/pp3ppp/2p5/q3Pb2/1nP5/N7/PP1B1PPP.text:
The threat of a discovered check is bigger, so White has to defend against that.

But their nightmare is just beginning.

We'll take on e5 with check.

rn1Nk2r/pp2p1bp/2p3p1/8/2BP4/5b2/PPP2PPP.text:
White will take ours.

And we can keep capturing, on g2.

rn1Nk2r/pp2p1bp/2p3p1/8/2BP4/8/PPP2PbP/R.text:
White attacks the bishop and the material will soon be equal.

We'll take the knight first.

rn1k3r/pp2p2p/2p3p1/8/2Bb4/8/PPP2PRP/R1B.text:
And there's a free pawn in the center.

All White's tactic does is to trade a lot of pieces. The position remains in the balance.

We've won a pawn but the position is wide open and the bishop pair and our exposed king gives White some compensation.

rn1q1rk1/pp2ppbp/2p1b1p1/3nN3/2BP4/2P5/P.text:
White is also trying to complete development, but tension will soon arise.

The knight on e5 is very active and challenging it is a good idea.

rn1qk2r/pp2pNbp/2p3p1/3b4/2BP4/5Q2/PPP2P.text:
They can capture on f7.

We can't recapture the knight because the bishop covers that square as well.

So we'll take the queen instead.

rn1qk2r/pp2ppbp/2p1b1p1/3NN3/2BP4/5Q2/PP.text:
White captures.

And we'll take back with the bishop.

In this line, we allowed White a tactic.

rn1qkb1r/pp2pp1p/2p1b1p1/3nN3/2BP4/2N2Q2.text:
A trade will be offered at some point, but we don't have to be the ones who capture.

We can finish development instead.

rn1qkb1r/pp2pppp/2p5/4Nb2/1nPP4/N3B3/PP3.text:
Once that is defended...

We can offer a trade of knights, now that our other knight is stable on b4.

White has to be careful now.

rn2kb1N/pp2p1pp/2p5/5b2/2P1q3/P1N5/1P2BP.text:
White has to get the knight out to save it here.

Why are we winning?

Simply put, our knight on a1 will be able to escape, while White's won't.

That's why trading queens and simplifying the position is a great idea.

rn2kb1N/pp2p1pp/2p5/8/2P5/P1N5/1Pb1BPPP/.text:
And we'll take back with the bishop.

While our knight can easily escape to b3, we'll play ...g6 and ...Bg7 on the kingside to capture White's trapped one.

Black will be up a piece and winning.

rn2kb1N/pp2p2p/2p3p1/5b2/2P5/P7/1P1NBPPP.text:
We can play ...g6 and ...Bg7 is coming, as in the other line.

White won't be able to save the knight.

rn2kb1r/pp3ppp/2p1p3/4qb2/1PP5/8/1P2BPPP.text:
We'll open up the dark-squared bishop.

In the end, we've won a pawn but the position is unclear.

The engine recommends the crazy c5 Bxb1!? here.

rnb1kb1N/pp2p1pp/2p5/8/2P1q3/P7/1P2BPPP/.text:
Sure, White can take our rook and think the position is equal...

But we've got all the momentum.

We'll play Bf5. This is better than taking on b1, when Bd3 would give White dangerous play.

rnb1kb1N/pp2p1pp/2p5/8/2P5/P7/1P2BPPP/nN.text:
We'll lose ours, but our ideas remain simple and effective.

First, the bishop comes out to f5 to attack the knight.

rnb1kb1r/pp2pNpp/2p5/8/1nP1q3/P7/1P2BPPP.text:
If White blocks with the bishop here, we've proved our point of placing the knight on b4.

We can simply fork them on c2.

rnb1kb1r/pp2pNpp/2p5/8/1nP1q3/P7/1P2QPPP.text:
Blocking with the queen doesn't change much.

We've still got the fork on c2, and this line is even more painful for White.

rnb1kb1r/pp2pNpp/2p5/8/1nPq4/P7/1P3PPP/R.text:
Another possibility is a desperado by White.

Instead of trading the knights by capturing ours first, they want to sacrifice on f7.

But this move is a mistake: we've got an intermezzo of our own.

Suddenly, the queen finds itself on e4 from where it controls the c2-square, which is crucial.

rnb1kb1r/pp2pNpp/2p5/8/2P1q3/P7/1Pn1BPPP.text:
The king slides to f1.

And we'll just take the rook in the corner.

rnb1kb1r/pp2pNpp/2p5/8/2P1q3/P7/1Pn1QPPP.text:
The king has to sidestep.

First, we'll trade the queens.

rnb1kb1r/pp2pNpp/2p5/8/2P5/P7/1Pn1BPPP/R.text:
Once White recaptures...

We'll get that rook.

rnb1kb1r/pp2pppp/2p5/4N3/1PPq4/8/1P3PPP/.text:
One of the other options White has is to take our knight.

We'll simply capture the white knight on e5.

rnb1kb1r/pp2pppp/2p5/4q3/1PP5/8/1P2BPPP/.text:
The bishop blocks the check...

And we'll continue developing.

rnbq1rk1/pp2ppbp/2p3p1/3nN3/2BP4/2P5/PP3.text:
White improves their structure.

Our short-term plan is to get our queenside pieces out and trade for White's active ones.

rnbqk2r/pp2ppbp/2p3p1/3nN3/2BP4/8/PPP2PP.text:
White centralizes the rook and adds protection to the knight.

Let's get castled.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pp1p/2p3p1/3nN3/2BP4/5Q2/PPP.text:
If White goes for the double attack, we know the defense already.

We'll place the bishop on e6 and cover both threats.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pp1p/2p3p1/3nN3/2BP4/8/PPP2P.text:
Castling is pretty natural.

We'll fianchetto, and prepare for castling as well.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/2p5/3nN3/2BP4/8/PPP2PPP.text:
6.Bc4 is the more common move here, played 32% of the time.

White finishes kingside development and puts more pressure on the center.

Similarily to the previous chapter, we'll go for the kingside fianchetto.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/2p5/3nN3/2PP4/8/PP3PPP/.text:
The more aggressive c4 is played 24% of the time, and it leads to more complicated positions.

The main difference is that we're jumping to b4 this time, not retreating to b6.

We've got a tactic in mind, as you will see.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/2p5/4N3/1nPP4/4B3/PP3PP.text:
White could choose the calmer approach and simply develop and protect the d-pawn.

This doesn't mean we will take our foot off the gas.

First, we will activate our bishop to f5 and threaten to jump to c2.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/2p5/4N3/1nPP4/P7/1P3PPP.text:
If White tries to attack our knight right away, which I'm sure you will face a lot, this is where we can implement our tactic.

We can just capture on d4!

If White captures our queen, we've got ...Nc2+ to get it back.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/3p4/3nP3/3P4/5N2/PPP2P.text:
White abstains from the usual c4 and decides to develop the knight immediately.

The move-order actually matters in the early Alekhine.

We will encounter similar positions but with key differences.

4.Nf3 is played 24% of the time, in more than 1.3 million games.

We'll trade pawns.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/8/3nN3/3P4/8/PPP2PPP/R.text:
White will recapture with the knight.

Here, I recommend supporting the knight on d5 with ...c6.

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/5n2/4P3/8/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
White attacks the knight.

d5 is the square now.

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/8/3nP3/3P4/8/PPP2PPP/R.text:
A natural move in the center to support the structure.

Let's challenge it right away.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
Chapter 4 will deal with White playing d4, but opting not to go for c4.

This allows for quicker development by White and early aggression without spending a move to attack the knight again.

White could also choose to play c4 at a later point which leads to tricky positions.

Let's get started with 1. e4 Nf6!

2kr1b1r/ppp1q2p/1nn1pp2/8/2P3bB/5N2/PPQ1.text:
And we will finally castle queenside.

As mentioned, we will use the rook on the g-file if we want to attack.

Our structure is a bit shaky on the kingside but now there's space to develop the dark-squared bishop too.

r1k2b1r/ppp2ppp/2n1p3/4P3/1nP2Bb1/N4N2/P.text:
The king simply slides to c8 and there is no danger.

Since White has castled queenside, we would like to reactivate our bishop on f5, where it would serve a greater purpose.

Meanwhile, our dark-squared bishop can attack the now vulnerable f2-pawn.

Black is substantially better.

r2k1b1r/ppp1pppp/2n5/4P3/1nP2Bb1/N4N2/PP.text:
That's why White has to protect the pawn.

Now it's time to get the dark-squared bishop out.

r2qkb1r/ppp1pppp/2n5/3nP3/6b1/5N2/PPP1BP.text:
White chooses to castle.

Our dark-squared bishop could use some breathing space.

r2qkb1r/ppp2ppp/1nn1p3/4P3/2P3b1/5N2/PPQ.text:
White's queen gets out to c2.

They could have also traded, but that would have given us some activity.

We're expecting Rd1 to attack our queen, so let's get it out of the way.

r2qkb1r/ppp2ppp/2n1p3/3nP3/2P3b1/5N2/PP2.text:
But now White attacks our knight.

Moving to b4 in this instance doesn't prove to be effective.

There is no bishop on d3 to attack and we wouldn't be threatening anything, so we'll go back to b6.

r3kb1r/ppp1q1pp/1nn1pP2/6B1/2P3b1/5N2/PP.text:
White captures on f6.

We don't mind recapturing with the g-pawn; on the contrary, it will open up the g-file, which we'll use to attack later.

r3kb1r/ppp1qppp/1nn1p3/4P1B1/2P3b1/5N2/P.text:
White might think they've got us when they play Bg5 here, attacking the queen.

This looks uncomfortable, but we have a nice defensive resource in the form of f6.

r3kb1r/pppq1ppp/2n1p3/3nP2b/2B5/3Q1N1P/P.text:
And we will follow up with our plan.

Our pieces are active and we want to castle long.

There is also the threat of capturing on f3 and then on e5.

rn1Qkb1r/ppp1pppp/8/4P3/1nP3b1/5N2/PP3PP.text: And they will get traded, most likely.

rn1k1b1r/ppp1pppp/8/4P3/1nP3b1/N4N2/PP3P.text:
White doesn't have many options but to play Na3.

Let's get the other knight into the game and put pressure on the e5-pawn.

rn1q1rk1/ppp1bppp/1n6/3p4/3P2b1/1BP2N2/P.text:
And we'll get the bishop out, pinning their knight.

The position is equal with natural development to follow.

You can support the center with  ...c6 or look to advance on the queenside with ...a5.

Playing for ...c5 could also be an idea.

rn1qkb1r/ppp1pppp/8/3nP3/2B3b1/5N2/PPP2P.text:
Thanks to 5.dxe5, the White queen was already attacking our knight, and now they add another attacker.

So let's protect it.

rn1qkb1r/ppp1pppp/8/3nP3/2P3b1/5N2/PP3PP.text:
However, you have to be ready for c4 at any point.

We can place our knight on b4 in case the queens get traded and there is a fork opportunity on c2.

rn1qkb1r/ppp1pppp/8/3nP3/6b1/5N2/PPP1BPP.text:
A line White could go for is Be2, simply unpinning and defending.

This means White wants a traditional game with simple development and castling.

Let's keep an eye on the e5-pawn. and continue developing our pieces with Nc6.

rn1qkb1r/ppp2ppp/4p3/3nP3/2B3b1/5N2/PPP2.text: White castles, and I suggest an unorthodox approach here, where we aim to castle queenside.

rn1qr1k1/1pp2ppp/3p1b2/p4b2/1nPP4/N4N2/P.text:
We can simply protect it with ...a5.

White capturing on b4 is always good for us as it opens up the a-file.

Apart from that, they can't target any of our pieces.

Black is slightly better because of the mighty bishops.

rn1qr1k1/ppp1bppp/3p4/5b2/1nPP4/N4N2/PP2.text:
White stops it with Na3, which already looks passive.

The dark-squared bishop could use some improvement right now.

rn1qr1k1/ppp2ppp/3p1b2/5b2/1nPP4/N4N2/PP.text: White attacks the knight, but we don't have to move it.

rn2kb1r/pppq1ppp/4p3/3nP2b/2B5/3Q1N1P/PP.text: They choose to activate the queen instead and unpin.

rn2kb1r/pppq1ppp/4p3/3nP3/2B3b1/5N1P/PPP.text:
If White attacks the bishop, nothing to worry about.

We'll retreat and maintain the pin.

rnbq1rk1/ppp1bppp/1n6/3p4/3P4/1BP2N2/PP3.text: White decides to support the center...

rnbq1rk1/ppp1bppp/3p4/3n4/3P4/3B1N2/PPP2.text:
And White does the same.

The bishop on d3 does slightly restrict our development, as it covers the f5-square.

But we've got a plan for that.

First of all, let's place our rook on the open e-file.

rnbqk2r/ppp1bppp/1n1p4/8/3P4/1B3N2/PPP2P.text:
The bishop will most likely retreat to b3, and this is the freedom we get in this variation.

Nothing prevents us from pushing ...d5!

rnbqk2r/ppp1bppp/3p4/3n4/2BP4/5N2/PPP2PP.text:
A somewhat confrontational move is Bc4, and you always have to look out for it.

White tries to get a tempo by attacking our knight.

We'll retreat and attack the bishop.

rnbqk2r/ppp1bppp/3p4/3n4/3P4/3B1N2/PPP2P.text:
Developing to d3 keeps the position calm.

Let's get the king into safety.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/3P4/3n4/3P4/8/PPP2PPP/.text:
White could choose to relieve the tension immediately.

This poses no threat to us whatsoever and we can continue logically.

This move is played 13% of the time, in almost 750,000 games.

We'll recapture with the e-pawn and make room for our bishop to come to e7.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/3p4/3nP3/3P4/5N2/PPP2P.text:
We've already covered some lines after 4.Nf3, but not all of them. 

Black's best choice is to trade.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/8/3nP3/8/5N2/PPP2PPP/R.text:
What if they capture with the pawn?

This move is played just under 45% of the time, so expect to see it a lot.

White wants to keep a pawn deeper in our camp and has some flexibility from here.

We'll utilize a very common idea in the Alekhine, and pin the g4-knight.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/3p4/3n4/3P4/5N2/PPP2PPP.text: Once they activate the knight, we'll bring out our f8-bishop.

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/5n2/4P3/8/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
Attacking the knight.

Let's jump forward.

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/8/3nP3/3P4/8/PPP2PPP/R.text:
White expands with d4.

Let's challenge the center.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
Study 2 will look into the rare lines of the d4-only setup.

Specifically, we'll cover the early exchange on d6, where White allows for pretty natural development.

We will also look into White recapturing with the pawn on e5, which leaves them with multiple options later on.

White opens with e4, and we'll reply with Nf6.

rnbqr1k1/ppp1bppp/3p4/3n4/2PP4/3B1N2/PP3.text: Once our knight is attacked, we are not going to retreat, seeing as we can attack the bishop on d3.

rnbqr1k1/ppp1bppp/3p4/8/1nPP4/5N2/PP2BPP.text:
Once it retreats to e2, the f5-square is in our hands again.

Our bishop can occupy it, and threaten to win the rook on a1 with ...Nc2.

r1b1k3/p1Bp1p2/2n1p2p/1pb1P3/7P/2P5/PP2B.text:
But the engine move here is 14...b5.

15.Bxb5 Bb7 is already -1 in our favor, though we probably can't play Rxf2 in most circumstances because of b4 to bother our rook's defender.

This is an odd line but something you may see at higher level of play.

r1bBk1r1/pppp1p2/2n1p2p/2b1P3/2B3QP/2P5/.text:
White takes our queen.

We'll, of course, take theirs.

r1bBk3/pppp1p2/2n1p2p/2b1P3/6rP/2P5/PP2B.text:
The bishop has to move away from the attack.

And now the g2-pawn is hanging.

r1bq1rk1/pp2bppp/2npp3/3nP3/2BP4/5N2/PP2.text:
White centralizes their rook.

Let's keep developing the queenside.

r1bqk1r1/pppp1p1p/2n1p3/2b1P1B1/2B3QP/2P.text:
White can play 11.h4 to defend.

And we play ...h6.

r1bqk2r/pppp1p1p/2n1p3/2b1P1B1/2B3Q1/2P5.text:
The bishop grabs the pawn.

Now we bring the rook into the action and pin it.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n1p3/2b1P3/2B2BQ1/2P5/.text:
This is a challenging line. 

If your opponent plays it, they are probably quite a strong player.

Let's check out this crazy line.

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n1p3/2P1P3/2B2B2/2P5/.text: White defends, but the c5-pawn is now free.

r2q1rk1/pp1bbppp/2n1p3/4P3/2B5/2P2N2/P3Q.text: White recaptures and opens up their rook on d1.

r2q1rk1/pp1bbppp/2npp3/3nP3/2BP4/2N2N2/P.text:
The knight goes to c3 and attacks our d5-knight.

We don't mind trading, even if White gets another c-pawn.

r2q1rk1/pp1bbppp/2npp3/4P3/2BP4/2P2N2/P3.text:
White recaptures.

Our plan now will shift: through trades, we can create a situation where White has an isolated c-pawn.

r4rk1/ppqbbppp/2n1p3/4P3/2B5/2P2N2/P3QPP.text:
And we get out of the d-file. 

The engine thinks we're equal, but I really like our endgame chances, in particular vs the long-term weakness on the c-file. 

We will play ...Rfd8 and ...Be8 to let our rook be active on the d-file. We can even play a rook lift to double rooks on the d-file.

rn1qkb1r/pp2pp1p/2p3p1/2PpP3/8/2PB1Q1P/P.text:
We will play ...Bg7, Nd7 and ...e6. 

Moves like ...a5 are also possible at some point to expand on the queenside. We have a very stable position with play for both sides.

rn1qkb1r/pp2pppp/2p5/2PpP3/6b1/2PB1N1P/P.text:
White may pressure us to trade. 

Since we have strong pawns on light squares, we don't need the light-squared bishop so much as our pawns inhibit its mobility.

rn2kb1r/pp3ppp/8/3pP3/3P2bq/8/PP4PP/RNBQ.text:
We will play ...Nc6 and Bb4. 

If 12.Nf3 Bxf3 is good for us. In some positions, ...0-0-0 adds a needed defender to d5, although the plan of ...0-0 and f6 is also solid.

rnb1kb1r/pp3ppp/8/3pP3/3P3q/8/PP4PP/RNBQ.text:
White has to give up castling rights. 

We have an advantage.

rnbq1rk1/pp2bppp/3pp3/3nP3/2BP4/5N2/PP2Q.text:
The queen is developed.

We need to bring out the queenside.

rnbq1rk1/pp3ppp/3b4/3pN3/3P4/8/PP3PPP/RN.text:
This position is dead equal. White has obtained nothing from the opening and we're solid. 

We can play a timely ...f6. ...Be6 is a sound way of defending d5, but you may even consider Bxe5 in some positions. 

You shouldn't shy away from trading the bishop for the strong central knight.

rnbqk2r/pp2bppp/3pp3/3nP3/2BP4/5N2/PP3PP.text:
White castles first.

We should as well.

rnbqk2r/ppp2ppp/3b4/8/8/2P5/PP3PPP/R1BQK.text:
We have an equal position. 

We want to play the rook to e8 and develop our knight. 

White hasn't achieved anything.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/2p5/2PpP3/8/2PB1N2/PP3P.text:
The game could now continue like this, given the structure: 

White develops their bishop, and we develop ours as well.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/3p4/3pP3/3P1P2/8/PP4PP/R.text:
Adding another pawn to the mix may seem like a good idea. 

After all, White wants to build a big center.

We can chip away at the center for the advantage.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/3p4/3pP3/3P4/5N2/PP3PPP/.text:
With this move, White defends their center.

We should take on e5 to get rid of our doubled d-pawns and to give our dark-squared bishop more room.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/3pp3/3nP3/2BP4/5N2/PP3PP.text:
This is the most popular move now. 

White simply develops and supports their center.

Our main goal is to castle quickly.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/8/3pN3/3P4/8/PP3PPP/RNBQ.text:
The knight recaptures.

We can start putting some pressure on the knight.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/8/3pP3/3P4/8/PP4PP/RNBQK.text:
The f-pawn recaptures, and this gives way to a common tactical pattern, due to the h4-e1 diagonal being open.

10.dxe5 would have allowed us to play our bishop to c5.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/3P4/4P3/8/2P5/PP3PPP/R.text:
7.exd6 isn't popular at all because players want to undouble their c-pawns and trade a flank pawn for a central one.

Recapturing with the e-pawn allows the dark-squared bishop to get out.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/8/2PpP3/8/2P2N2/PP3PPP.text:
White could simply ignore our pawn.

Which means we get to keep our pawn on d5.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/3P4/3pP3/3P4/8/PP3PPP/R.text:
White captures towards the center.

8.exd6 gives up a central pawn without necessity and so it isn't a good move for White.

Of course, we'll recapture.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/3P4/8/8/2P5/PP3PPP/R1BQ.text:
It is very common for White to simply continue trading down pawns. 

8.Nf3 ...Nd7 puts pressure on e5.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/3Pp3/3nP3/2BP4/8/PP3PPP.text:
White prefers to take with the c-pawn in the majority of cases.

We'll recapture.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/3pp3/2P1P3/2B5/2P5/P2P1.text:
We should be calm and simply play ...d6. 

...Bxc5 was a dangerous move: it gives White time to create a big center with d4, and Qg4 is also an idea. 

We will play Nd7 to put pressure on the e5- and c5-pawns.

rnbqkb1r/pppp1ppp/4p3/2P1P3/2B5/2P5/PP3P.text:
Without White building a huge center after d4, we could consider taking on c5 at some point.

For now, we just develop and attack the e5-pawn.

rnbqkb1r/pppp1ppp/4p3/2PBP3/8/8/PP1P1PPP.text:
About 35% of games feature this capture. 

White gives up the bishop pair.

We take back on d5.

rnbqkb1r/pppp1ppp/4p3/2PnP3/2B5/2N5/PP1P.text:
A quarter of games go like this. 

White is giving up the c5-pawn for tricks. 

We have to trade on c3, since retreating isn't an option.

rnbqkb1r/pppp1ppp/4p3/2PnP3/2BP4/8/PP3PP.text:
23% of games go like this. 

White connects their pawns. We have to fight back and challenge their central structure.

rnbqkb1r/pppp1ppp/8/2PpP3/3P4/8/PP3PPP/R.text:
White connects their pawns.

We need to open things up in the center so our pieces have some freedom.

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/1n6/2P1P3/8/8/PP1P1PPP.text:
But 21% of games have seen the move 4.c5 here to attack our knight again.

Let's return right away to the d5-square!

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/5n2/4P3/8/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
Our knight is attacked.

We'll move it into the center.

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/8/2P1P3/8/2P5/PP3PPP/R.text:
6.dxc3 is the best recapture for White. 

It's good because White activates their queen along the d-file and also they open up their c1-bishop. 

Black should get active in the center.

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/8/2PnP3/2B5/8/PP1P1PPP.text:
Half of the games in the database feature this move. 

It's yet another attack on our knight.

...e6 will do the job.

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/8/2PnP3/8/2N5/PP1P1PPP.text:
White could propose a trade here. This happens about 20% of the time.

We don't have a better place for out knight, so we'll just trade.

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/8/3nP3/2P5/8/PP1P1PPP/.text:
3.c4 here happens about one third of the time.

b6 is a safe square for our knight.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
For this study, we will see White Play e4 and e5, followed by c4 and c5 without them playing d4 to connect these advanced pawns.

Some people do play d4 later on because it's hard to avoid this move. Let's check out the moves.

We begin with 1.e4 Nf6.

r1b1kb1r/pp2pppp/1nn5/8/2p5/2P2N2/PPBPKP.text:
We can enjoy a queenless middlegame where we've got more space and the advantage of greater activity.

Next, we should activate the light-squared bishop before playing ...e6.

Castling queenside is quicker and better here.

r1b1qb1k/ppp1p2p/1nnpP1p1/8/8/5Q2/PPPP1P.text: Not much they can do only with their queen out.

r1b1qbkN/ppp1p2p/1nnpP1p1/8/8/5Q2/PPPP1P.text:
White will probably capture.

We'll take their knight.

r1bq1rk1/pp2bppp/1nnp4/2p5/8/1B1P1N2/PPP.text:
But not for long.

We've got an equal position on our hands.

Still, the fact that we've prevented White from advancing with d4 is a big up-side to our position.

Next, I recommend finishing development and improving our pieces, with moves such as ...Bf6.

r1bqkb1r/pp1ppppp/1nn5/2p1P3/8/1B1P1N2/P.text:
White develops naturally and defends the e5-pawn.

We can continue undermining their structure.

r1bqkb1r/pp2pppp/1nnP4/2p5/8/1B1P1N2/PPP.text:
White captures.

We can recapture with the pawn here as enough pieces control the d4-square.

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/1nnp4/2p5/8/1B1P1N2/PPP2.text:
White decides to castle now.

We'll prepare to do the same.

r3qb1k/ppp1p2p/1nnpb1p1/8/8/5Q2/PPPP1PPP.text:
We'll capture on e6.

We've got two pieces for the rook and three active pieces.

Meanwhile, White has only gotten their queen out and castled.

A completely winning position for Black.

rnb1k2r/pp2bppp/2p5/3p4/8/1B3N2/PPPPnPPP.text:
Well, after we support the center, our plan is to capture the bishop on c1!

Once White moves the d-pawn, that bishop could become dangerously active.

This way, we remove it while White can't defend it!

We'll be left with the bishop pair and a comfortable position.

rnb1k2r/ppp1bppp/3p4/8/2B2n2/5N2/PPPP1PP.text:
And White castles.

The queens have been traded off, and we should look for as much activity and space as we can get here.

Do you see a move in the center we can play?

rnb1k2r/ppp1bppp/8/3p4/5n2/1B3N2/PPPP1PP.text:
The bishop retreats to b3 now.

There is another idea I had in mind after ...d5.

We can gain the bishop pair.

rnb1k2r/ppp1bppp/8/3p4/8/1B3N2/PPPPnPPP/.text: White has to move the king.

rnb1kb1r/pp2pppp/1n1q4/2p5/8/1BP2N2/PP1P.text:
White chooses to develop the knight instead.

But now it's time to shut the door on any d4 possibilities.

rnb1kb1r/pp2pppp/1n1q4/8/2p5/2P2N2/PPBP1.text:
The bishop retreats to c2.

I recommend we give a check here, since we want to trade queens in this line and remove White's castling rights.

rnb1kb1r/pp2pppp/1n2q3/8/2p5/2P2N2/PPBPQ.text:
They basically have to block with the queen.

Let's trade, according to plan.

rnb1kb1r/ppp1qppp/3p4/3n4/2B5/5N2/PPPPQP.text: If they block with the queen, we can actually play ...Nf4 here, which is much more powerful after the check we gave.

rnb1qbkr/ppp1p1pp/1n1pP3/6N1/8/5Q2/PPPP1.text:
Our position looks cramped after e6, and White is threatening mate in two with Qf7+ Qxf7 exf7#.

However, we are up a piece, and if we untangle ourselves, we will be winning. 

We'll play g6 and give our king some room.

rnb1qbkr/ppp1pN1p/1n1pP1p1/8/8/5Q2/PPPP1.text:
The best they can do is go after the rook.

We can't protect it, but we can use this chance to develop.

rnbq1b1r/ppp1pkpp/1n1p4/4P1N1/8/8/PPPP1P.text:
This is White's idea.

They want to check again and get the queen into the game next.

Watch out not to go back to e8.
If you do that, e6 is extremely strong for White.

rnbq1bkr/ppp1p1pp/1n1p4/4P1N1/8/5Q2/PPPP.text:
Now there's a checkmate threat.

However, it's defendable.

rnbqkb1r/pp1ppppp/1n6/2p1P3/8/1B1P4/PPP2.text: White could prevent our potential ...c4 with d3, controlling that square, so let's continue developing instead.

rnbqkb1r/pp1ppppp/1n6/2p1P3/8/1BP5/PP1P1.text:
Another option to save the bishop is c3.

White opens up the c2-square for the bishop and wants to play d4 later on, supported by the pawn.

Let's challenge the e5-pawn first, as one should in the Alekhine.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/1n1P4/2p5/8/1BP5/PP1P1P.text:
White captures.

I suggest recapturing with the queen here, as pushing d4 wil be harder for White.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pBpp/1n1p4/4P3/8/5N2/PPPP1P.text:
White can sacrifice the bishop with check.

We'll have to recapture. Otherwise, we are just much worse.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/1n1p4/4P3/8/1B3N2/PPPP.text: If White retreats, we are in known territory.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/3P4/3n4/8/5N2/PPPP1PPP.text:
White captures.

Recapturing with the e-pawn to open up the e7-square is good.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/3p4/3nP3/2B5/5N2/PPPP1.text:
White doesn't have to capture on d6 right away.

We'll retreat to b6, as per usual.

There is actually an interesting sacrifice here that you should watch out for.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/3p4/3n4/2B5/5N2/PPPP1PP.text:
Now the standard Bc4 arrives.

White is playing in Italian style, developing the knight and the bishop before anything else.

This piece-first approach has some merit to it.

...Qe7+ is a great reply here, making White decide between Qe2 or Be2.

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/1n6/4P3/8/1B6/PPPP1PPP.text:
White retreats to the most logical square.

We have a fun move up in our sleeve, threatening to trap the bishop.

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/5n2/4P3/8/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
White still pushes the pawn.

Let's get the knight out of the way.

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/8/3nP3/2B5/8/PPPP1PPP/.text:
The move 3.Bc4 is only played 7% of the time, but that is still a lot of games.

The point is that White wants to develop with tempo before grabbing space with the pawns.

We can grab a tempo back and attack the bishop.

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/8/3nP3/8/5N2/PPPP1PPP/.text:
White can choose to develop the knight before advancing in the center.

This unorthodox move-order is played 9% of the time, but that is still in almost 2 million games!

Our plan shouldn't change as much. Undermining the center is still good.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
Chapter 6 will deal with the rarer variations of the Alekhine.

Namely, those where White neither plays d4 nor c4.

Some players like to approach all positions from a similar standpoint, and that's worth exploring as well.

White opens with e4 and we'll reply with Nf6.

2kr1b1r/ppp1pppp/2n5/3q4/3P2b1/2P2N2/PP2.text:
Even if White defends with c3, they are not out of the woods. 

We have a strong resource with the central pawn break.

2kr1b1r/ppp1pppp/2n5/5q2/2PP2b1/5N2/PP2B.text:
And then we can castle.

The d4-pawn is a huge target now, especially with the vulnerable defender on f3.

Black is better.

2kr1b1r/ppp2ppp/2n5/3q4/3N2b1/2P5/PP2BPP.text:
The knight recapturing leads to some trades.

We'll take the bishop first.

2kr1b1r/ppp2ppp/2n5/3q4/3N4/2P5/PP2QPPP/.text:
White recaptures with the queen.

We'll trade the knights as well.

2kr1b1r/ppp2ppp/2n5/3qp3/3P2b1/2P2N2/PP2.text:
They can choose to run away, getting the king into safety.

But the d4-pawn is very tender.

Let's exchange pawns.

2kr1b1r/ppp2ppp/2n5/3qpb2/8/3PBN2/PPP1BP.text: The bishop comes out to e3, and this is where you should think about attacking.

2kr1b1r/ppp2ppp/8/3q4/3P4/8/PP2QPPP/R1B2.text:
Once White recaptures, there is a free pawn on d4.

But watch out not to grab it right away.

12...Qxd4 runs into 13.Bg5.

2kr1b1r/ppp3pp/2n2p2/3qpb2/8/3PBN2/PPP1B.text:
First, we will support the center.

Since the kings are castled on opposite sides, that usually only means one thing.

And that's a pawn storm!

Prepare to push those g- and h-pawns in the near future. Black is doing great.

2kr3r/ppp2ppp/3b4/3q4/3P4/8/PP2QPPP/R1B2.text:
Simply developing and connecting the rooks is better.

That pawn is isolated and is not going anywhere.

Now we are safe and have new fronts of improvement such as ...Rhe8.

Black is definitely better.

r1b1k2r/ppp2ppp/2n5/2b1q3/8/2P1B3/PP3PPP.text:
And we will take advantage of that with ...Bc5.

A great position for Black where the queen isn't challenged at all and we've got 3 pieces out already.

White has to defend here.

r1b1kb1r/ppp1pppp/2n5/3q4/3P4/4B3/PPP2PP.text:
White defends with the bishop.

But, in Scandi style, we can strike in the center with e5.

r1b1kb1r/ppp1pppp/2n5/3q4/3P4/5N2/PPP2PP.text:
When you see the pawn move to d4 in a position like this, think of it as a hook.

Our priority is to castle queenside as quickly as we can and push ...e5 to counteract White's advance.

We'll develop our bishop to g4, putting indirect pressure on d4.

r1b1kb1r/ppp1pppp/2n5/3q4/8/5N2/PPPPBPPP.text:
Another passive move by White.

It seems like they just want to castle and stay solid, giving us all the freedom in the world.

And we'll gladly take space in the center with e5!

r1b1kb1r/ppp2ppp/2n5/3qP3/8/4B3/PPP2PPP/.text:
Most players will capture here.

It's better to keep our queen active and in the center than trade queens.

r1b1kb1r/ppp2ppp/2n5/3qp3/8/5N2/PPPPBPPP.text:
White castles.

Next, we'll finish our queenside development, with queenside castling coming.

r1b1kb1r/ppp2ppp/2n5/4q3/8/2P1B3/PP3PPP/.text: White defends the b2-pawn, but their bishop on e3 is still pinned.

r1b2rk1/pp3ppp/1nnqp3/2p5/8/1B1P1Q2/PPP1.text:
We will recapture with the queen.

Expect to see Bf4 at some point to attack your queen.

Apart from that, we have got a lot of potential with the knights on c6 and b6.

r1bq1rk1/pp2ppbp/2n3p1/2p5/2BP4/2P1BN2/P.text:
But we'll attack it once more.

The position is still equal, but it's important to stay flexible and know which lines require you to implement the ...g6, ...Bg7 and ...c5 approach.

r1bq1rk1/pp3ppp/1nn1p3/2p5/5Q2/1BNP4/PPP.text:
White recaptures.

Their pieces are very active.

r1bq1rk1/pp3ppp/1nnNp3/2p5/8/1B1P1Q2/PPP.text: White usually claims the bishop pair.

r1bq1rk1/pp3ppp/1nnbp3/2p5/5B2/1BNP1Q2/P.text:
White might try to trade off our strong dark-squared bishop with Bf4.

We don't mind trading.

r1bq1rk1/pp3ppp/2n1p3/2pn4/5Q2/1BNP4/PPP.text:
But we counter that by centralizing the knight.

White either has to move the queen or trade, which works in our favor.

The position is equal.

r1bqk2r/pp3ppp/1nnbp3/2p5/4N3/1B1P1Q2/PP.text:
A sharp move is definitely Ne4.

White improves the knight and goes after our active bishop.

Moving it away saves it but loses some important time.

Instead, we'll get our king into safety.

r1bqk2r/pp3ppp/1nnbp3/2p5/8/1BNP1Q2/PPP1.text:
You could see castling here.

Which allows us to do the same.

r1bqkb1r/pp2pppp/1nn5/2p5/8/1BNP1N2/PPP2.text:
White can continue in a natural manner with Nf3.

We will also make a natural developing move.

r1bqkb1r/pp2pppp/1nn5/2p5/8/1BNP1Q2/PPP2.text:
The best move in this position, although rare, is actually Qf3.

It is annoying because White is threatening to capture on f7.

...e6 is the best defense, but it blocks our light-squared bishop.

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/1nn1p3/2p5/8/1BNP1Q2/PPP.text:
White continues with Nge2 since the f3-square is occupied.

We'll prepare to castle as well.

r2q1rk1/pp2bppp/1nn1p3/2p2b2/5B2/1BNP1N2.text:
And after a natural sequence from both sides, Black actually has the better position!

There is more potential for improvement in our position, with moves like ...a5, ...a4 and ...Na5 on the queenside to go after the bishop and ...Bf6 on the kingside.

Our c-pawn is doing a great job controlling the center and we can bring the rook to support it.

r2qk2r/pp2bppp/1nn1p3/2p2b2/5B2/1BNP1N2/.text:
The bishop comes out to f4 now.

Both sides simply improving.

r2qkb1r/pp2pppp/1nn5/2p2b2/8/1BNP1N2/PPP.text:
White castles.

The dark-squared bishop could use some breathing room, so we'll give it air with e6.

r2qkb1r/pp3ppp/1nn1p3/2p2b2/8/1BNP1N2/PP.text:
White centralizes the rook.

Let's prepare our king for castling.

r3kb1r/ppp1pppp/2n5/3q4/2PP2b1/5N2/PP3PP.text:
If your queen is attacked, it's important to know where to move it.

f5 is a good spot for the queen, as we have seen in some earlier studies.

r3kb1r/ppp1pppp/2n5/3q4/3P2b1/5N2/PPP1BP.text:
A passive but safe option is unpinning right away.

That allows our plan to move forward, though.

We castle.

r3kb1r/ppp1pppp/2n5/5q2/2PP2b1/5N2/PP2BP.text: White will have to unpin at some point.

r3kb1r/ppp2ppp/2n5/3qpb2/8/3P1N2/PPP1BPP.text:
There aren't many active moves White can make.

In order to open up one of the bishops, they have to block the other one.

We'll castle queenside.

rn2kb1r/ppp1pppp/4b3/3q4/8/5Q2/PPPP1PPP/.text:
We will let them, but on our own terms.

If they capture, our bishop will be a monster in the center.

Besides, we will get the knight out and castle long in no time.

rnb1kb1r/ppp1pppp/8/3q4/3P4/8/PPP2PPP/R1.text:
If White chooses to expand in the center, we can make that pawn a target.

Let's start by developing our knight and attacking the d-pawn.

rnb1kb1r/ppp1pppp/8/3q4/8/5N2/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
If White goes for Nf3 here, that shouldn't change our plans a lot.

As long as our queen isn't under attack, we should continue developing the queenside.

rnb1kb1r/ppp1pppp/8/3q4/8/5Q2/PPPP1PPP/R.text: If White really wants to trade as many pieces as possible...

rnbq1rk1/pp2ppbp/6p1/2p5/2BP4/2P1BN2/P1P.text: Probably the best they can do is develop and protect the center.

rnbq1rk1/ppp1ppbp/6p1/8/2BP4/2P2N2/P1P2P.text:
Once they castle too, we are about to demonstrate how the bishop on g7 can come to life.

Let's play to undermine the white center, starting with c5.

rnbqk2r/ppp1ppbp/6p1/8/2BP4/2P2N2/P1P2PP.text:
They want to castle as well.

We are first, though.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/1n6/2p5/8/1BNP4/PPP2PPP.text:
White defends with d3, also opening up the bishop.

We'll just keep developing.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pp1p/6p1/8/3P4/2P2N2/P1P2PP.text:
White advances with d4, of course.

Let's get the dark-squared bishop where it belongs.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/1n6/8/8/1BN5/PPPP1PPP/.text: White retreats to b3, and Chapter 6 might hint at the next move you should play.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/3P4/8/2N5/PPPP1PPP.text:
Study 1 will deal with White capturing on d5, which is the most common move and played almost 45% of the time.

This equals to more than 3.3 million games.

White doesn't want to complicate matters by pushing and simply exchanges pawns.

We'll take back, bringing our knight into the center of the board.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/8/3N4/8/8/PPPP1PPP/R1B.text:
The move you will see by far the most is Nxd5.

It is simply logical for White to trade their c3-knight for our knight in the center.

This move is played almost 60% of the time.

Our queen replaces the knight in the center of the board.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/8/3n4/2B5/2N5/PPPP1PPP.text:
Another move White can play is Bc4, developing with tempo.

This move is played 13% of the time.

We have to either move or protect the knight.

I don't think capturing on c3 is the best here because we give up our only active piece, so we'll retreat to b6 and hit the bishop.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/8/3n4/8/2N2N2/PPPP1PPP.text:
The move Nf3 does nothing about the knight tension and is played 12% of the time.

Since White has allowed it, let's capture on c3.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/8/8/8/2P2N2/P1PP1PPP/R.text:
The c-pawns are doubled, but White is preparing d4.

I suggest letting them expand in the center and going for the fianchetto here.

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/5n2/8/4P3/2N5/PPPP1PPP.text:
Already, White doesn't play the expected 2.e5.

This means that either they are unprepared, or think you are.

Black goes for a completely different approach here!

We'll push in the center with d5. Note that e5 instead transposes into the Vienna.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
Chapter 7 will deal with a very specific approach by White, which is signified by the move 2.Nc3.

Already on move 2, White chooses not to push the pawn on e5 and play the traditional Alekhine but rather defend it with the knight.

You might face this from players who want to avoid known theory or transpose into different openings.

Let's begin with 1.e4 Nf6.

r1b1k2r/pp1n1ppp/1qn1p3/2bpP1B1/N7/5N2/P.text:
Expect to face this fork a lot.

White players just can't wait to attack your queen and your bishop like this.

However, this is a mistake!

Do you see a tactic?

We can capture on f2 with check!

r1b1k2r/pp1n1ppp/1qn1p3/3pP1B1/N7/5N2/PP.text:
White has to accept this sacrifice.

And now we have a fork on b4!

r1b1k2r/pp1n1ppp/2n1p3/3pP1B1/1q6/2N2N2/.text: Sure, White can retreat and block...

r1b1k2r/pp1n1ppp/2n1p3/3pP1B1/8/2N2N2/Pq.text:
But now the b2-pawn falls and there is another fork, since the knight on c3 isn't defended anymore.

Our sacrifice on f2 was actually a deflection of the White queen.

Black is winning.

r1b1kb1r/2qn1ppp/p1p1p3/3pP3/3B4/2N2N2/P.text:
We'll recapture with the pawn, of course.

We've got possibilities of pushing ...c5 now, as well as ...d4 after it.

We should grab space this way.

On the kingside, we'll develop the bishop and castle.

Black is much better.

r1b1kb1r/pp1q1ppp/1n6/1B1PP1B1/3n4/8/PP3.text:
But we can simply take the white queen. As White will take ours in return, this is in effect a trade of queens.

We emerge a piece up, with an easily winning position.

r1b1kb1r/pp1q1ppp/1nn1p3/1B1NP1B1/2PQ4/8.text:
White castles, but can't save the knight.

We simply take it.

r1b1kb1r/pp1q1ppp/1nn5/1B1PP1B1/3Q4/8/PP.text: White recaptures with the pawn, hitting our c6-knight.

r1b1kb1r/ppqn1ppp/2n1p3/1B1pP3/3B4/2N2N2.text:
White decides to castle.

Let's kick the bishop out with a6.

r1bqk2r/1p1n1ppp/p1n1p3/2BpP3/5Q2/2N2N2/.text:
White doesn't have much of a choice.

We'll recapture.

r1bqk2r/1p1n1ppp/p1n1p3/2bpP3/5P2/2NB1N2.text:
We'll give our c5-bishop some breathing room instead.

Before castling, watch out for potential Greek Gift sacrifices by White.

Apart from that, both sides have active pieces and although White has more space, we've got potential too with moves like ...Ba7 and ...Nc5.

r1bqk2r/1p3pp1/p1n1p2p/2npP3/5Q2/2NB1N2/.text:
This is a dynamic position with fireworks to come from both sides.

We need to be careful when castling kingside as White has many pieces pointing towards it.

A plan like ...h6-Qc7-Bd7-b5 would be a good idea.

r1bqk2r/1p3ppp/p1n1p3/2npP3/5Q2/2NB1N2/P.text: And now the bishop comes out to d3.

r1bqk2r/p2nbppp/2p1p3/2ppP3/3P4/2N2N2/PP.text:
And a calm developing move by us to end the line, preparing castling.

There is still tension in the center and despite White removing an attacker, we will definitely go after those pawns on d4 and e5.

We still don't mind if White captures on c5 at any point.

r1bqk2r/pp1n1ppp/2n1p3/2bpP3/5P2/2NB1N2/.text:
White gets the bishop out.

We would like to castle, but there's danger.

r1bqkb1r/1p1n1ppp/p1n1p3/3pP3/5Q2/2N1BN2.text:
White quickly castles long, which is one of the benefits of recapturing with the queen on d4.

They do have a lot of active pieces,   which is why some exchanges could be good for us.

We'll propose a trade on c5.

r1bqkb1r/pp1n1ppp/2B1p3/2ppP3/3P4/2N2N2/.text:
In this line, White probably played Bb5 with the intention of capturing on c6.

That knight was an important piece after all.

Naturally, we'll take back.

r1bqkb1r/pp1n1ppp/2n1p3/1B1pP3/3B4/2N2N2.text:
White can attack our knight as much as they want.

We'll just support it with the queen, also eyeing the center.

r1bqkb1r/pp1n1ppp/2n1p3/3pP3/3B4/2N2N2/P.text:
And we will create a pawn chain.

This is actually a transposition to the 5.Nf3 variation, so you will know what to do if you learn that one.

r1bqkb1r/pp1n1ppp/2n1p3/3pP3/5Q2/2N1BN2/.text:
However, White's plan is to slide to f4 and keep an eye on the e5-pawn.

But we've got enough time to play a6, preventing a piece from coming to b5 and disrupting our knights.

r1bqkb1r/pp1npppp/2n5/2ppP3/3P4/2N1BN2/P.text:
They will most likely keep defending.

Now it's time to capture.

r1bqkb1r/pp2pppp/1nn5/1B1NP3/2PQ4/8/PP3P.text:
Now c4 comes to the defense of the d5-knight.

But we just attack the knight again with ...e6.

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/1nn1p3/1B1NP1B1/2PQ4/8/P.text:
As we also see in the 7.c4 line, White tries to attack our queen and provoke ...Qxg5, which would lead to Nc7+.

But the calm Qd7 maintains the pin.

Even our knight on c6 is no longer pinned to the king.

rnb1k2r/pp1n1ppp/1q2p3/2bpP1B1/8/2N2N2/P.text:
White defends it.

Capturing on b2 isn't good here because White gets Rb1 and Nb5 with a lot of activity.

We'll develop instead.

Now the e5-pawn is under pressure and there is no pawn defending it.

rnb1k2r/pp1q1ppp/1n2p3/3NP1B1/1bPQ4/P7/1.text: If White attacks our bishop here, no worries.

rnb1kb1r/pp1n1ppp/1q2p3/2PpP1B1/8/2N2N2/.text:
White captures on c5 first to relieve the tension.

We'll take with the bishop.

Now the f2-pawn is under pressure as well.

rnb1kb1r/pp1q1ppp/1n2p3/3NP1B1/2PQ4/P7/1.text:
We can just move all the way back.

White can't save the pinned knight now, and we're completely winning.

rnbqk2r/pp1n1ppp/4p3/2bpP3/5P2/2N2N2/PPP.text:
White slides all the way back.

Now it's time for us to grab some activity, developing further with Nc6.

rnbqk2r/pp3ppp/1n2p3/3NP1B1/1bPQ4/8/PP2K.text:
So they move the king.

There is no castling now.

We can play ...Qd7 and maintain the pin.

rnbqkb1r/pp1n1ppp/4p3/1BppP3/3P4/2N2N2/P.text:
Bb5 is a move you have to look out for, as it can come at any moment.

The good thing is that our response to it almost always stays the same.

And that is ...Nc6.

We block the bishop's pin and attack the center.

rnbqkb1r/pp1n1ppp/4p3/2ppP1B1/3P4/2N2N2/.text:
A move that we need to treat with precision is Bg5.

We don't want to play ...Be7 because if the dark-squared bishops get traded, White can infiltrate with Nb5-Nd6.

That's why ...Qb6 is a must.

We get out of danger and attack the b2-pawn.

rnbqkb1r/pp1n1ppp/4p3/2ppP3/3P4/2N1BN2/P.text:
One of the logical options is 6.Be3, providing more support to the center.

However, White needs to really know what they're doing in order for this to work.

We'll take on d4 and pose the question as to how they will recapture.

rnbqkb1r/pp1n1ppp/4p3/3pP3/3B4/2N2N2/PPP.text:
White recapturing with the bishop gives us a clear plan.

We'll play Nc6, and Black is already better here.

A simple plan is to push ...a6, develop the queen to c7 and the bishop to e7.

rnbqkb1r/pp1n1ppp/4p3/3pP3/3N4/2N1B3/PPP.text:
Recapturing with the knight is an obvious mistake.

We'll just take the free pawn.

rnbqkb1r/pp1n1ppp/4p3/3pP3/3Q1P2/2N2N2/P.text:
White continues to develop naturally, but their pieces won't stay active for long.

Take a look at the c5-square.

We can activate the bishop to there and attack the queen!

Developing while pushing White's pieces back is certainly the way to go.

rnbqkb1r/pp1n1ppp/4p3/3pP3/3Q4/2N1BN2/PP.text:
The best move is to actually recapture with the queen.

But it seems illogical to do so when you've just played Be3.

That's why this move is only played 3% of the time!

We'll immediately develop and attack the queen with Nc6.

rnbqkb1r/pp1npppp/8/2pNP3/3P4/8/PPP2PPP/.text:
One is to capture the free pawn on d5.

This is actually a mistake, as you will see.

And White players make it 23% of the time.

We'll take on d4 first.

It is crucial to tear apart White's center.

rnbqkb1r/pp1npppp/8/2ppP3/3P1P2/2N5/PPP3.text:
White could choose to be aggressive and protect the e5-pawn.

This is played 16% of the time.

The downside is that the d4-pawn is vulnerable.

And we'll capture it.

White would love to recapture with a pawn, but they can't.

rnbqkb1r/pp1npppp/8/2ppP3/3P4/2N1B3/PPP2.text:
Defending the pawn with the bishop is definitely an option, although a little bit passive-looking.

It's played 16% of the time.

We will continue attacking the pawn, with Nc6.

White shouldn't capture because that would render the e5-pawn unstable.

rnbqkb1r/pp1npppp/8/2ppP3/3P4/2N2N2/PPP2.text:
White going for Nf3 is the most common move here, played 25% of the time.

They want to defend the center before they capture on d5.

It's better to play ...e6 here and guard the d-pawn, awaiting White's next developing move.

rnbqkb1r/pp1npppp/8/3NP3/3Q4/8/PPP2PPP/R.text:
The queen recaptures, and suddenly White is losing.

After our reply of Nb6, their knight is pinned on d5!

It is not easy for them to get away from this.

rnbqkb1r/pp1npppp/8/3pP3/3Q1P2/2N5/PPP3P.text:
Instead, the queen comes out to d4.

Our d5-pawn is under attack now.

So we'll defend it in the most natural way, with e6.

White could try to play Bb5 here, but it only results in ...Nc6.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/1n6/1B1NP3/3Q4/8/PPP2PP.text:
One way they could try is to give a check with the bishop first.

But a simple ...Nc6 blocks it.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/1n6/3NP3/2PQ4/8/PP3PPP/.text: A move like c4 seems natural, but don't forget we can attack the knight just as easily with e6.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/1n2p3/3NP1B1/2PQ4/8/PP3P.text:
White could try and counter attack our queen.

The point is that if we take the bishop, there is Nc7+ and Qd6#.

And if we move the queen to d7, White wants to castle long and somehow defend.

So the best move is the counter check ...Bb4+!

White can't capture the bishop because the knight is pinned.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/2n1p3/1B1p4/3N4/2N1B3/PP.text:
As we just go back and we've simply won a pawn.

White has no compensation for it.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/3pP3/8/2N5/PPPP1PP.text:
And now White pushes the pawn.

This move grabs space and comes with tempo, so we have to move the knight.

Expect to see this move 38% of the time, as it was played in almost 2.8 million games.

White is also preparing d4.

We retreat to d7, attacking the pawn.

rnbqkb1r/pppnpppp/8/3pP3/3P4/2N5/PPP2PPP.text:
The most natural way to defend it is d4.

But we will strike back immediately, with ...c5!

It turns out that placing the knight on c3 isn't the best for White as they can't reinforce the center with c3.White has got a lot of options here.

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/5n2/8/4P3/2N5/PPPP1PPP.text:
The knight comes out to c3.

We strike in the center with d5.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
The second study of Chapter 7 will take a look at the second option White has on move 3, and that is 3.e5.

It certainly makes as much sense to push the pawn and attack the knight as it does to capture, it my opinion.

White opens with e4, as always, and we'll reply with Nf6.
